profile.clarity_reason: We know the product (protein bars) and the pitch (taste); only price, audience and model are unstated and defaulted.
assumptions: Assumed a mid price tier and roughly $35 first order, typical for a protein bar multipack.
Assumed a broad adult audience of 25-44, any gender.
Assumed one-time purchases rather than a subscription.

picks.name: The Fitness Enthusiast
picks.why_plausible: Works out 4+ times a week and buys supplements and recovery products, so protein bars are already in the basket; price_sensitivity low-medium fits a mid-tier $35 order.
lean_into: post-workout fuel that fits a training routine
avoid: fake athlete endorsements the brand can't back
picks.ad_angle: The post-workout bar you'll actually look forward to — protein that performs without the chalky punishment.

picks.name: The Wellness Optimizer
picks.why_plausible: Category affinities include supplements, fitness and wellness with low price sensitivity, so she buys protein bars routinely. She's disinterested in ultra-processed food, so the ad must lead with ingredient honesty rather than candy-bar hype.
lean_into: no cardboard, no compromise on what's inside
picks.ad_angle: You shouldn't have to choose between a clean ingredient list and something that tastes good.

picks.name: The Convenience-First Millennial
picks.why_plausible: Defaults to whatever is easy and stocks up on repeat purchases; the brief's audience is explicitly people who eat protein bars for convenience. Medium price sensitivity fits a $35 mid-tier box.
picks.ad_angle: The fastest lunch you'll ever eat — and the first one you won't regret.

picks.name: The Gen Z Aesthete
picks.why_plausible: Responds to playful brand voice, which is the advertiser's only stated value, and buys functional beverages and impulse snacks. Medium-high price tolerance at a $48 typical AOV.
picks.ad_angle: Lead with the joke: protein bars that don't taste like cardboard — said out loud, with attitude.

picks.name: The Busy Parent
picks.why_plausible: Time-poor, convenience-motivated and buys snacks in bulk for the household; medium price sensitivity fits mid tier. Taste matters because kids and adults both have to actually eat it.
picks.ad_angle: A grab-and-go snack the whole house will actually eat — no half-finished bars in the backpack.

candidates.detail: shops impulse, wellness≈functional_beverages, fitness≈functional_beverages; responds to playful
shops snacks≈natural_food, wellness≈natural_food; price-mismatched for mid

plan.summary: No competitors here, so the plan leans on fitness and functional-wellness audiences (Studiogrid, Movewell, Pop & Sip) plus a boosted convenience-grocery test at Swiftcart for impulse snacking, while apparel, pet, beauty and home publishers fall away as off-category.

test.name: Pop & Sip
test.adjustment_reason: Notes describe the audience as "Health-curious but indulgence-seeking", which is almost exactly the taste-first protein bar buyer; the category score (38) understates that.
test.rationale: Pop & Sip sells better-for-you drinks to people who still want it to taste good, and shares the playful tone; $42 typical order makes a $35 bar box an easy add.

evidence.quote: Health-curious but indulgence-seeking. Strong overlap with wellness and premium grocery

test.risk: Only 5.2M impressions, so volume will be modest even at a good conversion rate.

test.name: Swiftcart
test.adjustment_reason: Notes say "High-frequency purchasers" and "Impulse-friendly", and the publisher sells groceries — this is the single best impulse-snack context in the catalog, which a 26 category score badly undersells.
test.rationale: Swiftcart's convenience buyers already purchase snacks on impulse at a $28 typical order, and 84M monthly impressions is the largest reach available; the only thing dragging the score down is an abstract "no shared values".

evidence.quote: High-frequency purchasers. Late-night traffic spike. Impulse-friendly

test.risk: 18-34, mid-income convenience shoppers are price-sensitive; a $35 multi-bar box is above their $28 habitual basket.

test.name: Studiogrid
test.rationale: Studiogrid's notes say users are "actively spending on self-care and fitness", so a post-class confirmation page catches people already in a fitness mindset, and the $42 typical order sits right next to a $35 bar box.

evidence.quote: Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

test.risk: Bookings are services, not consumables, so buyers may not be in a shopping mindset at confirmation.

test.name: Movewell
test.rationale: Movewell's "Fitness-engaged shoppers" at 22M monthly impressions is the largest genuinely on-category audience here, and its 25-44 age skew matches the brand's assumed 25-44 target exactly.

evidence.quote: Fitness-engaged shoppers. Strong crossover with wellness and beauty

test.risk: A $78 apparel order makes a $35 snack purchase feel like a small afterthought; 82% female skew narrows reach for a unisex bar.

excluded.name: Pantrygood
excluded.rationale: Pantrygood shoppers buy natural snacks, but they are "Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims" — none of which this taste-first brand makes.

evidence.quote: Values-driven shoppers. Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

excluded.risk: A pitch built only on taste reads as thin to an ingredient-scrutinizing grocery audience.

excluded.rationale: Category overlap with supplements is real, but Daily Form is "Science-forward wellness" and this brand's whole pitch is that the bars "don't taste like cardboard" — a claim that won't satisfy a proof-seeking audience.

campaign.name: Protein bars marketed on taste · post-purchase launch

bid_strategy.rationale: $35 first order (assumed) × 0.30 = $10.50 target CPA: one-time purchase, so the first order has to pay back the acquisition. The max CPA allows headroom while the campaign learns over 14 days.

frequency_cap.rationale: Offers appear once, right after checkout; repeating them reads as spam.

experiment.graduate_rule: After 14 days, move a test publisher to core if its CPA is at or below target; cut any placement above max CPA.
experiment.notes: Creatives rotate evenly until each has enough conversions to compare.

assumptions: Assumed a mid price tier and roughly $35 first order, typical for a protein bar multipack.
Assumed a broad adult audience of 25-44, any gender.
Assumed one-time purchases rather than a subscription.
Allowable CPA is 30% of first order value (one time); replace with real margin and LTV.
warnings: No publisher cleared the recommended bar, so the whole budget is a test. Treat results as exploratory.
Target CPA is based on an assumed order value. Confirm price before launch.
